title: Practice Exam 1: Foundations & Core Integration
description: Foundational Messages API mechanics, token budgeting, tool execution loops, context ceilings, and baseline model routing.

questions.scenario: An engineering team is automating a customer mortgage verification process. The procedure requires four rigid, ordered steps: verify customer identity, pull credit scores, calculate debt-to-income ratio, and generate a compliance disclosure. The order of operations never changes and requires no dynamic exploration. Which architectural pattern should the team adopt?
options: A deterministic workflow pipeline that executes explicit API calls in a fixed sequence.
An autonomous agent loop where Claude determines tool invocation order dynamically.
A multi-agent hierarchical supervisor that delegates each step to distinct subagents.
An event-driven state machine managed through an external Model Context Protocol server.

rationales.correct: Option B is correct. When steps are deterministic and sequential, a standard code workflow pipeline is far cheaper, lower latency, and more reliable than an autonomous agent loop. The course states: decide workflow vs agent before writing the loop.
distractors: Option A is incorrect because an autonomous agent loop adds unnecessary non-determinism, token overhead, and routing latency to a fixed sequential task.
Option C is incorrect because multi-agent hierarchical orchestration introduces massive token multiplication (roughly 15x) without any architectural benefit for a linear task.
Option D is incorrect because an external MCP server is a tool connectivity interface, not an internal workflow execution orchestrator.

questions.scenario: A development team splits a tightly coupled, multi-file database refactoring task across five parallel subagents coordinated by a supervisor. The monthly token bill increases roughly fifteen-fold, while task completion quality remains unchanged compared to a single-agent run. What is the most proportionate architectural change?
options: Increase the per-turn token limit for each subagent to accelerate task resolution speed.
Revert to a single agent with curated context, reserving fan-out for independent parallel tasks.
Add three specialized subagents to divide the refactoring tasks into even smaller slices.
Enable output streaming on the supervisor agent to reduce perceived end-to-end task latency.

rationales.correct: Option A is correct. Multi-agent fan-out multiplies token costs (~15x) and only delivers value when work splits into truly independent parallel streams. On tightly coupled refactorings where subtasks depend on shared state, a single agent with good context engineering is more effective and far cheaper.
distractors: Option B is incorrect because raising subagent token limits further inflates token spend on tasks that are already failing to benefit from fan-out.
Option C is incorrect because adding more subagents to a coupled task compounds coordination friction and multiplies token consumption.
Option D is incorrect because streaming alters perceived latency for a human observer but does not address the underlying token multiplier or architecture flaw.

questions.keyInsight: Fan-out only pays when the task splits into independent parallel parts. On coupled tasks, orchestrator-worker patterns cause roughly 15x token multiplication with flat quality.

questions.scenario: An orchestrator agent equipped with a specialized code-review Skill delegates a submodule analysis to a child subagent. During execution, the subagent completely ignores the review checklist established in the orchestrator's session. What is the root cause?
options: The child subagent exhausted its context window and silently truncated the parent system prompt.
The parent orchestrator omitted the required beta header when dispatching the subagent task.
The child subagent starts with a clean context and inherits neither parent Skills nor session history.
The review checklist was written in Markdown rather than formatted as an executable tool schema.

rationales.correct: Option D is correct. Subagents are separate instances launched with a clean context window. They do not inherit the orchestrator's conversation history or loaded Skills. If a subagent needs a Skill, it must be explicitly configured in the subagent's own specification.

Option B is incorrect because beta headers govern API protocol features, not the inheritance of agent Skills.
Option C is incorrect because Agent Skills are legitimately defined in Markdown (SKILL.md); the failure is due to lack of inheritance, not the format.

questions.scenario: A developer authors a custom validation skill in `.claude/skills/lint/SKILL.md`. The skill activates smoothly in interactive Claude Code sessions. However, in an automated Python script using the Claude Agent SDK (`claude-agent-sdk`), the agent fails to discover or execute the skill. How should the developer resolve this?
options: Include the experimental `skills-2025-10-02` feature flag in the SDK client initialization options.
Move the skill declaration from `SKILL.md` into the root-level project `CLAUDE.md` instructions file.
Add `disable-model-invocation: false` to the frontmatter of the validation skill definition file.
Pass explicit `setting_sources=["user", "project", "local"]` in the `ClaudeAgentOptions` configuration.

rationales.correct: Option A is correct. In the Claude Agent SDK, `setting_sources` (or `settingSources` in TypeScript) is not populated by default. It must be explicitly configured with `["user", "project", "local"]` so the SDK knows to discover and load project-level skills and CLAUDE.md files.
distractors: Option B is incorrect because moving skill logic into CLAUDE.md inflates every single prompt context turn instead of leveraging modular on-demand skill execution.

Option C is incorrect because `disable-model-invocation: true` prevents autonomous model invocation, but omitting it or setting it false does not cause the SDK to discover skills when setting_sources is unconfigured.
Option D is incorrect because the issue is Agent SDK configuration discovery, not an unrecognized API beta header.

questions.scenario: An autonomous banking support agent executes database lookups, balance inquiries, and financial account transfers. To prevent unauthorized money movement while preserving automated responses for read-only tasks, where should the human approval gate be placed?
options: Inside the tool execution loop, intercepting irreversible actions immediately before invocation.
Immediately after tool execution, asking a human reviewer to validate the returned confirmation.
At session initialization, requiring user sign-off on the agent's proposed general action plan.
In a nightly asynchronous audit queue that flags completed reversal transactions for review.

rationales.correct: Option C is correct. The human-in-the-loop (HITL) gate must sit inside the execution harness loop immediately BEFORE executing irreversible or state-modifying tools (like transfers or edits). Checking before invocation prevents unwanted side effects, while allowing safe read tools to proceed without disruption.
distractors: Option A is incorrect because up-front sign-off cannot anticipate the exact tool inputs or arguments Claude might construct three turns later.
Option B is incorrect because placing the gate after tool execution means the financial transaction has already completed; the irreversible side effect has already occurred.
Option D is incorrect because asynchronous retroactive audits do not prevent unauthorized transactions in real time.

questions.scenario: A customer onboarding assistant conducts multi-session interactions spanning several weeks. By session four, concatenating all previous raw conversation transcripts into the request context consumes 40,000 tokens before the user enters a prompt. How should multi-session agent memory be implemented?
options: Increase the model's `max_tokens` allocation to ensure room remains for incoming prompts.
Persist state externally and inject a concise summary of prior sessions at session start.
Switch the model tier to Claude Opus to benefit from an expanded raw context window.
Enable prompt caching across all historical turns using default ephemeral breakpoints.

rationales.correct: Option B is correct. Concatenating raw transcripts across sessions is an anti-pattern that quickly saturates the context window and inflates costs. The course pattern: write state and key facts to external storage at session completion, and inject a synthesized summary into the context at session start.
distractors: Option A is incorrect because `max_tokens` controls generation output limit, not input context capacity.
Option C is incorrect because moving to Opus increases per-token costs without addressing exponential transcript bloat.
Option D is incorrect because prompt caching saves compute on matching prefixes, but concatenating growing transcripts still consumes cumulative context budget and degrades model focus.

questions.scenario: A digital health platform is designing an automated patient triage agent handling Protected Health Information (PHI). Corporate legal mandates a signed HIPAA Business Associate Agreement (BAA) and Zero Data Retention (ZDR). Why must the engineering team deploy a custom agent loop rather than Anthropic Managed Agents?
options: Managed Agents execute tools client-side, exposing internal healthcare network endpoints.
Managed Agents enforce strict rate limits that prevent multi-turn clinical data processing.
Managed Agents require passing credentials in plain text within prompt instructions.
Managed Agents maintain stateful server-side sessions that are ineligible for BAA or ZDR.

rationales.correct: Option D is correct. Anthropic Managed Agents maintain stateful agent execution environments stored server-side on Anthropic infrastructure. Option B is incorrect because compliance eligibility is governed by data retention architecture, not rate limit quotas.
Option C is incorrect because Managed Agents do not require credentials to be sent in plaintext prompt instructions.

questions.scenario: A customer service bot with 190,000 tokens of accumulated history generates output until it hits the model's context ceiling mid-generation. During development with short prompts, this never happened. What behavior does the API exhibit?
options: The API returns the generated text so far with stop reason `model_context_window_exceeded`.
The API raises an immediate 400 validation error before any tokens are returned.
The API silently purges the oldest conversation turns and completes the generation successfully.
The API returns an empty text block with stop reason `max_tokens` and an error message.

rationales.correct: Option A is correct. The context window has two distinct edge behaviors: (1) if input is already larger than the window, it is rejected with a validation error before generation begins; (2) if input fits but generation reaches the ceiling, Claude returns the generated tokens so far with stop reason `model_context_window_exceeded` without throwing an exception.
distractors: Option B is incorrect because a 400 error occurs only when the initial input payload already exceeds the context window prior to generation.
Option C is incorrect because the context window is a fixed budget; Claude never silently drops old conversation turns.
Option D is incorrect because `max_tokens` indicates reaching the requested completion limit, not the total model context window ceiling.

questions.keyInsight: The context window has two edge behaviors: input > window errors before generation; reaching the ceiling mid-generation returns output so far with `model_context_window_exceeded`.

questions.scenario: A client integration processes user queries through the Messages API. A specific prompt triggers content safety boundaries, resulting in an HTTP 200 response with `stop_reason: "refusal"`. How should defensive integration code handle this event?
options: Catch the exception, wait two seconds, and retry the identical prompt payload.
Inspect `stop_reason == "refusal"`, log the event, and halt without retrying blindly.
Check `stop_reason == "end_turn"`, strip the safety warning text, and display the rest.
Treat HTTP 200 as successful generation and parse the response body as normal content.

rationales.correct: Option B is correct. A refusal is a content decision returned at HTTP 200 (not an HTTP error status). The application must inspect `response.stop_reason`, log the refusal, and handle it gracefully. It should never silently retry, as the identical request will be refused again.
distractors: Option A is incorrect because a refusal is not a transient rate limit or network error; retrying blindly will repeatedly fail and consume quota.
Option C is incorrect because the stop reason is `refusal`, not `end_turn`.
Option D is incorrect because treating a refusal as normal structured output will cause parsing crashes downstream.

questions.scenario: A production system configured with `model="claude-sonnet-4-6"` suddenly experiences output formatting anomalies when Anthropic updates the alias to a newer point snapshot. Which practice prevents such unannounced production disruptions?

Retries cannot fix output shape drift when the underlying model response format has changed.

Paraphrasing adds latency and cost without guaranteeing injection neutralization.
Encoding text in hexadecimal obscures semantic meaning and degrades task performance.

questions.scenario: An agent's database lookup tool throws an unexpected connection timeout exception. The developer catches the exception and returns a `tool_result` with empty content `""`. Users now report that the agent produces confident, incorrect hallucinations. What is the correct fix?

Terminate the entire agent conversation loop immediately with an unhandled exception.

distractors: Tight loops without backoff can hammer struggling dependencies.
Terminating the session turns a recoverable tool error into an application outage.
Tool results belong in the user turn matching the tool call, not in the system prompt.
